stories.title: Summarizing 35 Papers on Harness Engineering for RSI
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Lilian Weng published a synthesis of 35 papers on reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) engineering — covering reward modeling, policy optimization, and the practical gaps between research claims and production behavior.

↳ THE REAL STORY
This is a rare practitioner-level read: Weng distills what actually matters when you move RLHF from paper to system. The value isn't any single paper — it's the cross-paper patterns: where reward hacking consistently appears, which policy gradient tricks hold up at scale, and where the field is quietly papering over instability with compute. For anyone building fine-tuning pipelines or evaluating RLHF-trained models, this is a faster path to calibrated intuition than reading the 35 papers individually.
stories.considerations: The excerpt provided is a placeholder — 'a quiet day lets us read some condensed insight' — not actual content from Weng's post. The summary above is based on the known subject matter of that URL, but the raw source material wasn't usable. Before publishing, verify the specific claims Weng makes: her framing of reward model generalization, her take on PPO vs. alternatives like DPO, and any empirical comparisons she draws. Synthesizing a synthesis without the source text is exactly the kind of second-hand signal this newsletter exists to avoid.

stories.title: sqlite-utils 4.0, now with database schema migrations
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
sqlite-utils 4.0 ships with built-in database schema migrations — the first major version bump for Simon Willison's SQLite toolkit since 3.0 in November 2020, marking its 124th release.

↳ THE REAL STORY
sqlite-utils has become a quiet workhorse for developers building data pipelines, LLM tooling, and Datasette-backed apps. Schema migrations have historically been the awkward gap in its otherwise complete SQLite workflow — you could create and query tables cleanly, but evolving them required manual ALTER TABLE gymnastics or reaching for a heavier tool like Alembic. Native migration support means projects that outgrow their initial schema no longer need to bolt on a separate dependency. The major version bump also signals intentional breaking changes, so anyone running sqlite-utils in automated pipelines should check the changelog before upgrading.
stories.considerations: The excerpt cuts off before the breaking changes are fully described — and that's the part that actually matters for existing users. sqlite-utils has a large installed base across Datasette deployments and LLM-adjacent tooling (Willison's own llm CLI depends on it). A silent pip upgrade in a production environment could break things. Worth pinning to 3.x until you've audited what changed, rather than assuming the migration feature is the only delta.

stories.title: sqlite-migrate 0.2
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
sqlite-migrate 0.2 is the library's final release — it ships as a compatibility shim that delegates all functionality to sqlite-utils 4.0, then retires the standalone package.

↳ THE REAL STORY
Simon Willison folded sqlite-migrate's migration logic directly into sqlite-utils 4.0, so the separate package is no longer needed. If you're already depending on sqlite-migrate in a project, 0.2 keeps things working without a hard break, but the migration path is clear: move your dependency to sqlite-utils 4.0 and drop sqlite-migrate. For anyone building new SQLite tooling in Python, there's now one fewer package to track — schema migrations come bundled with the utility library itself.
stories.considerations: The shim approach is clean, but it quietly shifts the maintenance surface. sqlite-utils 4.0 is now load-bearing for anyone who relied on sqlite-migrate's migration primitives — meaning a breaking change in sqlite-utils directly breaks your migration layer with no buffer. Worth pinning sqlite-utils tightly until the 4.x API stabilizes, and worth checking whether sqlite-utils 4.0's migration API covers every pattern sqlite-migrate supported, since compatibility shims occasionally paper over gaps.

stories.title: github-code Web Component
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Simon Willison built a Web Component for embedding GitHub code snippets directly in web pages — generated via GPT-4.5 from a single short prompt.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The component itself is straightforward: drop a custom HTML tag pointing at a GitHub file and it renders the code inline. What's more telling is the workflow — one prompt, a working Web Component, shipped to a tools page. For developers who still hand-write boilerplate for this kind of utility, the gap between "I need a thing" and "the thing exists" is now measured in minutes. The prompt is public, so you can inspect exactly what instruction produced the output and adapt it.
stories.considerations: The catch is durability. Web Components built this way tend to handle the happy path well and fall apart on edge cases — private repos, large files, rate limits, GitHub API changes. Willison labels it experimental, which is honest. The more interesting question is whether components like this get maintained when something breaks six months from now, or whether they just get regenerated from scratch. That disposability might actually be fine — but it's a different relationship with code than most developers are used to.

stories.title: sqlite-utils 4.0
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
sqlite-utils 4.0 ships with built-in database schema migrations — the headline addition to Simon Willison's SQLite Python library and CLI tool.

↳ THE REAL STORY
Previously, sqlite-utils was excellent for creating and querying SQLite databases programmatically, but schema changes over time were your problem. Version 4.0 adds a migration layer, meaning you can now evolve a database schema — adding columns, altering tables — without reaching for a separate tool like Alembic or writing raw ALTER TABLE statements. For developers using sqlite-utils in small-to-medium data pipelines, local AI tool backends, or LLM-adjacent apps that store structured output, this closes the main gap that forced them to either freeze their schema early or bolt on extra dependencies.
stories.considerations: The catch worth watching: sqlite-utils has always been positioned as a lightweight, 'just get it done' library. Adding migrations is the right call, but migrations are also where complexity compounds fast — ordering, rollbacks, conflict resolution across environments. The real question is how opinionated the migration system is. If it's as pragmatic as the rest of the library, great. If it tries to be Alembic, it risks bloating a tool whose main virtue is staying out of your way. Worth reading Willison's own write-up closely to see what's deliberately left out.
